Naive round-to-nearest quantization treats weights uniformly, applying the same scale to a group regardless of their individual impact. scenario.user_message: Explain speculative decoding and when it stops helping.
scenario.notes: Gains depend on acceptance rate; a poor draft model is a net loss.

results.response:
Speculative decoding accelerates generation by using a smaller "draft" model to propose a sequence of tokens, which a larger "target" model then verifies in a single forward pass. This approach avoids the sequential bottleneck of generating one token at a time, effectively batching multiple predictions into one computation step. Importantly, this is not an approximation; by following a modified rejection-sampling rule, the output distribution matches exactly what the target model would produce on its own [Leviathan et al., ICML 2023].

However, the technique stops helping when the draft model becomes inefficient relative to the gains. While increasing the number of proposed tokens theoretically allows more parallel work, the number of accepted tokens grows sublinearly because every new token depends on all previous ones being accepted. Conversely, the computational cost of running the draft model grows linearly. Once the draft length passes a certain threshold, the extra work required to generate the proposals outweighs the savings from skipping target model calls, meaning additional speculation is essentially paid for and discarded [Leviathan et al., ICML 2023].

Given that trade-off, how might you choose the optimal size for a draft model without knowing your target model's inference latency beforehand?

Rotary Position Embeddings work by rotating the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their absolute position.
